misattribution.description: From Jan 2026, 3 SG-coded duplicate records (created by SG staff, blank tax ID) captured POs of 2 Malaysian and 1 Vietnamese hospitals: C-SG-00074 “Hosp Taman Seri” is really Hospital Taman Seri (C-MY-00066); C-SG-00075 “Hosp Permatang Sutera” is really Hospital Permatang Sutera (C-MY-00004); C-SG-00076 “Song Sen International Hospital” is really Bệnh viện Quốc tế Sông Sen (C-VN-00035). Raw SG gains a level of S$1.1M over the 12 months; MY loses 4.7% and VN 4.5% of their 12-month value. This is the level shift the clean × method test detects.

examples.title: An SG-coded customer is really a Malaysian hospital
examples.rawStory: Raw: C-SG-00074 “Hosp Taman Seri” was created in SG on 2026-01-07 with a blank tax ID; from Jan 2026 it books S$481k of POs a year to Singapore, which looks like SG growth.
examples.dedupStory: De-duplicated: it is Hospital Taman Seri (C-MY-00066), a Malaysian hospital. SG gives back S$481k; MY gets 3.5% of its 12-month value back.

examples.title: A top-2 account is shrinking, hidden behind a 'new' customer
examples.rawStory: Raw SAP records: C-MY-00029 “Bukit Damai Specialist Hospital” (SPD) stops ordering after Mar 2026, so it looks lost; C-MY-00061 “Specialist Hospital Bukit Damai” (QTS) looks flat; C-MY-00091 “Bukit Damai Spec Hospital” (SPD) first orders in Apr 2026, so it looks like a new customer.
examples.dedupStory: De-duplicated: 3 records are one customer, Bukit Damai Specialist Hospital, #2 in Malaysia by 12-month PO value (S$1.1M), down 32% year on year (S$1.6M → S$1.1M).

examples.title: A hospital that looks like two half-customers
examples.rawStory: Raw: C-TH-00001 “Sri Chaloem Hospital” (SPD) buys only Product A from SPD and C-TH-00063 “Si Chalerm Hosp” (QTS) buys only Product C from QTS, so it looks like an A-only and a C-only customer, each a cross-sell lead.
examples.dedupStory: De-duplicated: one hospital, Sri Chaloem Hospital, already buys A and C; the real gap is Product B (lab consumables), which it buys from nobody in the group.

examples.title: A Vietnamese hospital's orders were booked to Singapore

records.cardName: Bệnh viện Quốc tế Sông Sen

examples.rawStory: Raw: from Jan 2026 most of Bệnh viện Quốc tế Sông Sen's orders go to SG-coded C-SG-00076 “Song Sen International Hospital”, so C-VN-00035 looks like a declining VN account and VN loses S$414k in the 12 months.
examples.dedupStory: De-duplicated: one hospital, Bệnh viện Quốc tế Sông Sen, in Vietnam. VN gets back 4.5% of its 12-month value; the romanised name and blank tax ID are why a name match alone would miss it.

examples.title: Two spellings of one Myanmar hospital
examples.rawStory: Raw: C-MM-00023 “Aung Myittar Hospital” (SPD), S$162k over 12 months, and C-MM-00038 “Aong Myitta Hospital” (QTG), S$50k, are two separate customers on two entities.
examples.dedupStory: De-duplicated: one hospital, Aung Myittar Hospital, worth S$212k over 12 months across SPD and QTG; Burmese names have no single romanisation, so spelling alone cannot find it.

note: Merging duplicate customers alone does not change country × product totals. Only the misattributed value (SG-coded records for MY/VN hospitals, from Jan 2026: S$1.1M in the 12 months) and the miscategorised value (reagent test kits coded as Product B: S$350k, of which TH S$276k, MM S$9k, VN S$65k) move between cells. SG's raw record count includes the 3 SG-coded records that belong to MY/VN customers. Duplicates do change customer counts, account rankings and the growth bridge (a 'lost' plus a 'new' customer becomes one shrinking account). The de-duplicated view uses the synthetic data's ground-truth golden IDs; the matcher that would build them in production is scored separately on held-out countries.
